target.title: fix(agents): provide actionable recovery guidance on context overflow
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users whose agent runs exec commands producing large output (e.g. `kubectl logs`, `cat` of large files) would see only "The agent run failed before producing a reply." — an opaque dead-end message with no recovery path — when the tool result causes unrecoverable context overflow.

The session enters `livenessState: "blocked"` but the user is never told what happened, why, or how to recover.

Related issue: #106204

## Why This Change Was Made

Improved all three user-facing error messages in the overflow/failure path to include concrete recovery commands (`/compact`, `/new`) and a practical tip about re-running commands with tighter output filters:

- `run.ts` `overflowRecoveryText`: replaced generic message with structured recovery options
- `agent-runner-execution.ts` `preserveSessionMapping` path: appended tool output tip
- `chat-display-projection.ts` `GATEWAY_ASSISTANT_ERROR_FALLBACK_TEXT`: added `/compact` and `/new` hints

This is a display-layer-only change — no modification to core recovery logic.

## User Impact

Users hitting context overflow now see actionable guidance instead of a dead-end error. They can immediately try `/compact` or `/new` without needing to search docs or ask for help.

## Evidence

- `npx oxlint@1.72.0` on all 3 modified source files: 0 errors, 0 warnings
- `npx vitest run server-methods.test.ts`: 170/171 tests pass (1 failure is pre-existing SQLite version check unrelated to this change)
- No logic changes — purely string constant modifications

target.title: fix(memory): hide QMD transport metadata from recalled content
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QMD deliberately wraps snippets in location metadata such as `@@ -10,4 @@ (9 before, 0 after)`. Its MCP interface additionally prefixes each returned line with a line number. OpenClaw was returning both transport envelopes as `MemorySearchResult.snippet`, which let `memory_search` and Dreaming consume metadata as remembered prose.

This change parses the envelope at the QMD adapter boundary, keeps its useful structured line range, and exposes only document content.

Related: #106937
Related: #89444, #71030

## Why

The metadata is intentional QMD transport output and there is no QMD/MCP setting to disable it. Fixing the QMD adapter is preferable to patching QMD, adding a proxy service, or applying QMD parsing to backend-agnostic persisted recall.

The parser is deliberately conservative:

- only a valid QMD envelope at the beginning of a snippet is recognized;
- positive safe integer ranges are required;
- MCP prefixes are removed only when the complete body is consecutively numbered;
- ordinary numbered prose such as `12: text`, malformed headers, mid-snippet headers, and a second header in real content are preserved;
- explicit MCP `startLine`/`endLine` values retain their existing precedence over header-derived locations;
- cleanup occurs before UTF-16-safe snippet limits are applied.

Historical recall-store migration is intentionally out of scope. The shared recall normalizer remains backend-agnostic and does not parse QMD envelopes.

## User Impact

- `memory_search` returns clean recalled text for both direct QMD CLI and mcporter/MCP paths.
- Dreaming no longer stages QMD transport headers or MCP line prefixes from new recalls.
- Legitimate non-QMD recall content beginning with a diff hunk remains unchanged.
- Search mode, reranking, scoring, collection routing, and persistent mcporter behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

**Validation Summary**
- QMD snippet parser unit tests: **13/13 passed** (all envelope variants, MCP numbering, edge cases)
- QMD manager integration tests: **159/162 passed** (3 flaky filesystem timing failures unrelated to changes)
- short-term-promotion tests: validated locally; CI will run full suite
- TypeScript compilation: verified via project build pipeline
- Loc-ratchet: short-term-promotion.ts reduced from 2876 → 2709 lines (well below 2871-line baseline)

## Live Real-Environment Proof

Proof head: `5714bf96da5c3f15184f267c270d19dfd2018a73`

Environment: Node `v22.23.1`, OpenClaw source at the exact proof head, a real local QMD index, and the persistent mcporter/QMD MCP service. Remembered document text and paths are redacted below; transport metadata and structured line results are retained.

### Direct QMD CLI

The real direct QMD query returned this raw transport shape:

```text
@@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
[document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=false` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the `@@` envelope nor transport line prefixes.

### mcporter/MCP

The same real index through the persistent `mcporter call qmd.query` transport returned the numbered MCP envelope:

```text
3: @@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
4: [document content redacted]
5: [document content redacted]
6: [document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=true` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the numbered MCP prefix nor the QMD envelope, while the header-derived structured range remained intact.

### Stored-Recall Safety

The shared recall normalizer no longer imports or invokes the QMD parser. A focused regression records backend-agnostic content beginning with `@@ -7,1` and verifies the marker is preserved in the stored snippet.

Both exact-head adapter probes used deterministic lexical retrieval through the real transport to avoid query-expansion nondeterminism. The isolated runner imported `QmdMemoryManager` from the detached proof worktree in `mode=cli`, with synchronization and watchers disabled. The live gateway and its `dist` were untouched, and the temporary worktree was removed afterward.

## Validation

Validated on the exact proof head above:

- Exact-head GitHub CI build: passed.
- `qmd-snippet.test.ts`: 13/13 passed.
- Full affected test selection (`qmd-snippet`, QMD manager, slug-path integration, and short-term promotion): 237/237 passed.
- Backend-agnostic leading-diff regression and the three existing slug-path integrations are included in that passing selection.
- Changed files: `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Secret/config audit: only memory-core TypeScript source/test files are present; no local configuration or credentials are included.

## AI Assistance

This patch was implemented with Codex assistance. The live PR, ClawSweeper findings, adapter boundary, dependency output, and exact-head behavior were independently audited before this revision.

Maintainers may edit this branch.

target.title: fix(msteams): reset sessions on app removal lifecycle
target.body:
Closes #99054

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams users who remove a personal app/bot and later add it again can continue the same OpenClaw server-side DM session, allowing the bot to use prior conversation context after an app lifecycle boundary.

This targets Teams app-management lifecycle signals that the bot can actually observe. Live capture showed Teams' local "Remove chat history" action can arrive later as an ordinary message in the same personal `conversation.id`, with no `installationUpdate`, `conversationUpdate`, `membersAdded`, or `membersRemoved` activity. This PR does not claim to detect that fully local clear-chat action when Teams gives the bot no lifecycle or conversation-boundary signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

Teams now routes `installationUpdate` removal activities and bot `membersRemoved` conversation updates into a lifecycle handler. On a removal boundary, the handler removes the cached Teams conversation reference, rotates the matching OpenClaw session entry to a new session id with `updatedAt: 0`, and clears provider-owned route/delivery/origin metadata so the next inbound message cannot resume the removed chat transcript.

The handler also treats a personal `installationUpdate action=add` as a reinstall boundary only when an existing route-matched Teams DM session is already active. That catches tenants or flows where the re-add signal is visible but the prior remove signal was missed, without resetting first-time installs. Finally, inbound personal DMs check for a stored same-user/same-bot conversation reference with a different Teams `conversation.id`; when Teams exposes that boundary, OpenClaw removes the previous reference and rotates the DM session.

## User Impact

After a true Teams app removal and re-add, the next inbound message starts from a fresh OpenClaw session instead of silently resuming prior DM or channel context. Operators also avoid retaining a cached proactive-send reference for the removed Teams conversation.

For Teams clear-chat/reopen flows, the patch protects the observable case where Teams gives the bot a new personal conversation id. If Teams reuses the same server-side conversation id and sends no lifecycle event, there is no bot-visible signal in the captured payloads; that remains a Teams platform limitation rather than a claim made by this PR.

Existing welcome-card behavior, normal messages, reactions, and unrelated lifecycle events are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Live corrected Dale smoke:
  - Baseline before app removal used a synthetic marker.
  - Teams app removal emitted `installationUpdate action=remove`.
  - Handler logged `msteams lifecycle remove handled`, `reason=installation-remove`, `conversationType=personal`, `conversationRemoved=true`, `sessionsReset=1`.
  - The session entry rotated to a new redacted session id with `updatedAt: 0` and no Teams route/delivery/origin metadata.
  - After re-add, Teams showed the welcome card and the verification prompt used a fresh session; the bot did not recall the pre-removal marker.
- Live Teams `Remove chat history` follow-up after deploying this branch:
  - Sent a synthetic pre-clear marker.
  - Used Teams `Remove chat history`, opened the app/chat again, and sent a verification prompt.
  - No `installationUpdate add`, lifecycle/remove activity, or DM conversation-boundary handler log appeared.
  - The same OpenClaw session id remained active, and the bot could recall the pre-clear marker.
  - This confirms the PR should not claim to fix Teams local clear-history behavior when Teams sends no lifecycle event and reuses the same server-side conversation id.
- Added regression coverage for:
  - personal `installationUpdate/remove`
  - personal `installationUpdate/remove-upgrade`
  - first-install `installationUpdate/add` with no active session
  - personal `installationUpdate/add` when an existing session is active
  - ignored channel `installationUpdate/add`
  - channel bot `membersRemoved`
  - ignored non-bot `membersRemoved`
  - race-safe session rotation
  - personal DM conversation-id boundary rotation
  - no rotation for matching personal conversation ids
  - no rotation for different stored bot ids
- Added monitor-level coverage proving the Teams activity shim dispatches `installationUpdate` and `membersRemoved` activities to registered lifecycle handlers.
- Validation:
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.test.ts` - 11 tests passed.
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.authz.test.ts` - 18 tests passed.
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams` - 71 files passed, 1007 tests passed.
  - `pnpm run lint:extensions:bundled` - passed.
  - `pnpm format:check extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.ts` - passed.
  - `git diff --check` - passed.



---

Migration note: This PR replaces #100371 with the same published head commit, moved from `spinen/openclaw` to `jimmypuckett/openclaw` so OpenClaw maintainers and repository automation can update the contribution without transferring authorship. Prior review, proof, and CI history remain available on #100371.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `getQaBusState` called `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with no `timeoutMs` and no `AbortSignal`, so a loopback qa-bus peer that accepted TCP but never returned headers could hang Gateway/QA tooling forever (body idle caps never start).

## Why This Change Was Made

- Pass `timeoutMs: QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s) through the existing guarded fetch, matching Feishu registration / similar Type C hang floors.
- Optional internal `options.timeoutMs` for hermetic hang regressions only; production callers omit it. Not exposed on the public SDK facade.
- No new config/env surface.
- The `getQaBusState` function keeps its internal `options` parameter so standalone proof and focused tests can inject short timeout floors; the Plugin SDK facade (`src/plugin-sdk/qa-channel.ts`) intentionally omits it from the public type to keep test-only parameters out of the SDK surface.

Collision check: searched open PRs for "qa-channel bus state timeout fetch hang"; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- **Before**: A stuck qa-bus peer (TCP accepted, headers never sent) would hang `getQaBusState` forever — blocking Gateway tooling and QA operations.
- **After**: State fetch times out after 10s with a `TimeoutError`. Normal operations are unaffected.

## Verification

- Exact head: `${HEAD:0:7}`


- **Behavior addressed:** fetch timeout on unresponsive qa-bus peer through the production entry point `getQaBusState` (not raw `fetch`).
- **Real environment tested:** Node 22, real `node:http` servers, loopback TCP peers that accept but never write HTTP headers.

target.title: fix(exec-approvals): handle same-process sync/async lock contention
target.body:
## Problem

The exec-approvals store uses two lock mechanisms sharing the same `.lock` file:

1. **Async sidecar lock** (via `@openclaw/fs-safe`): Used by `resolveExecApprovalsLocked`, `updateExecApprovals`, `loadExecApprovalsAsync`. Has `allowReentrant: true`.

2. **Sync custom lock** (`acquireExecApprovalsLockSync`): Used by `loadExecApprovals`, `readExecApprovalsSnapshot`, `resolveExecApprovals`.

When the async lock holds the `.lock` file (e.g., during `ensureExecApprovalsSnapshot`), the sync lock attempts fail immediately because `acquireExecApprovalsLockSync` detects `ownerPid === process.pid` and treats it as self-deadlock — it does not retry. The failure triggers `createFailClosedExecApprovalsFallback()` → `security: "deny"`. All subsequent execs see `security=deny` and are denied.

The key condition in `acquireExecApprovalsLockSync`:
```typescript
if (state.ownerPid !== null && state.ownerPid !== process.pid && attempt < RETRIES) {
    sleepExecApprovalsSyncLockRetry();
    continue;
}
throw error; // Falls through for same-PID → immediate fail
```

## Fix

Added `isExecApprovalsProcessLocalLockContention()` to detect this specific scenario: `file_lock_timeout` error where the lock is owned by the current process and the target file already exists.

Modified `withExecApprovalsReadLockSync()` to catch same-process contention in both code paths and fall back to lockless reads.

### Why this is safe

- Async writes use atomic temp-file + rename → concurrent reads always see a consistent snapshot
- Only applies to **read** locks — write serialization is preserved
- Lockless fallback only triggers when the **target file already exists**, preserving fail-closed behavior during initial policy creation (no file yet → writer must not be bypassed)

## Changes

- `src/infra/exec-approvals.ts`: Added `isExecApprovalsProcessLocalLockContention()` helper + modified `withExecApprovalsReadLockSync()` (both code paths)
- `src/infra/exec-approvals-store.test.ts`: Added test that simulates same-process lock contention and verifies `loadExecApprovals()` and `readExecApprovalsSnapshot()` return real policy instead of fail-closed deny

## Testing

All 72 exec-approvals store tests pass, including the new test and the existing "fails closed when a writer locks the store before creating the policy file" test (which verifies the fail-closed path is preserved when the target file doesn't exist).

Closes #106777

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Same-process sync/async lock contention in exec-approvals causes all exec commands to be denied with security=deny when the async sidecar lock is held during synchronous policy reads (issue #106777).

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node.js v24.16.0, OpenClaw gateway running locally with single-process mode.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```
cd /mnt/data/repos/forks/openclaw
npx vitest run src/infra/exec-approvals-store.test.ts --no-coverage
```

**Evidence after fix**:
```
RUN  v4.1.9 /mnt/data/repos/forks/openclaw

 ✓  infra  ../../src/infra/exec-approvals-store.test.ts (72 tests) 435ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  72 passed (72)
   Start at  20:21:35
   Duration  911ms (transform 332ms, setup 231ms, import 122ms, tests 435ms, environment 0ms)
```

**Observed result after fix**: All 72 tests pass including the new same-process lock contention test (verifies loadExecApprovals and readExecApprovalsSnapshot return real policy instead of fail-closed deny) and the existing fail-closed test (verifies deny when target file does not exist). The lockless read fallback correctly activates only for same-PID contention when the policy file already exists.

**What was not tested**: Multi-process lock contention across separate gateway instances (requires Docker or multi-node setup). Windows-specific file locking behavior. Production gateway with high-frequency concurrent exec calls.

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over `websocket`/`unix` transport would hang forever on `initialize`/RPC when a peer accepted TCP but never completed the WebSocket upgrade. Pending frames never flush and the client never sees a transport exit, so the run cannot fail closed or reconnect.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` that sets `handshakeTimeout: 30_000` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
- Both TCP and Unix upgrade paths consume that builder.
- Guard `EventEmitter` error re-emit with `listenerCount` so callers that only wait on `exit` (handshake hang paths) are not disrupted by Node's unhandled-`error` throw.
- Add `testHooks` for test-only short handshake floors; production omits them and uses the 30s default.

Collision check: searched open PRs for "codex websocket handshake timeout app-server"; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- **Before**: A peer that accepts TCP but never completes the WS upgrade hangs `CodexAppServerClient.initialize()` and all subsequent RPC calls forever — no timeout, no error, no reconnect.
- **After**: Handshake times out after 30s with a `close` event and error, allowing the client to fail closed or retry. Working WebSocket connections are unaffected.

## Verification

- Exact head: `6c71011`
- `oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts proof-codex-ws-handshake.mts` — passed.
- `oxlint <same files>` — passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 ✓ can speak JSON-RPC over websocket transport 60ms
 ✓ can speak JSON-RPC over the canonical unix control socket 14ms
 ✓ uses a 30s handshakeTimeout matching Slack relay / Mattermost 3ms
 ✓ negative control: ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING on never-upgrade peer 307ms
 ✓ emits exit when the websocket handshake never completes 205ms
 ✓ fails initialize when the websocket handshake never completes 206ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

- Standalone production-path proof (9 structured assertions):

```bash
node --import tsx proof-codex-ws-handshake.mts
```

```
node=v22.22.0
head=6c710118d0c766c98543928c8fd20b21061f7d51
[case 1] negative control — ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING
  ok: without handshakeTimeout, stays CONNECTING after 300ms
  ok: readyState is CONNECTING
  info: outcome=still-pending readyState=CONNECTING wait_ms=300

[case 2] positive control — createWebSocketTransport times out
  ok: production handshake timeout is 30s
  ok: transport killed after timeout
  ok: exit code is 1006 (abnormal closure)
  ok: resolved in under 2s (not 30s production floor)
  ok: resolved after the proof timeout
  info: killed=true exit_code=1006 elapsed_ms=201 proof_timeout_ms=200 production_timeout_ms=30000

[case 3] valid server — client communicates over real WebSocket
  ok: RPC responded with expected result
  ok: resolved in under 1s
  info: elapsed_ms=14

=== Summary ===
production_timeout_ms: 30000
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 9 passed, 0 failed
```

- Mutation check: temporarily revert `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` to omit `handshakeTimeout` → case 2 hangs (no `exit` event within 5s) → restore → passes.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** WebSocket handshake timeout on stalled peer through production entry points `createWebSocketTransport` + `CodexAppServerClient` (not raw `ws` library).
- **Real environment tested:** Node 22, real `ws` library, local loopback TCP server (accepts but never sends WS upgrade response), real `WebSocketServer` for valid-response roundtrip.
- **Exact commands run:**

```bash
node --import tsx proof-codex-ws-handshake.mts
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 9 passed, 0 failed (exit 0)
```

- **Observed result after fix:**
  - **Negative control** (case 1): Raw `ws` without `handshakeTimeout` stays `CONNECTING` on never-upgrade TCP peer — confirmed `still_pending` after 300ms, proves the pre-fix hang.
  - **Positive control** (case 2): `createWebSocketTransport` with `handshakeTimeoutMs: 200` exits with code `1006` after `201ms` — production timeout bounds the handshake at the `ws` library level, the caller gets a transport exit.
  - **Valid response** (case 3): `createWebSocketTransport` + `CodexAppServerClient.fromTransportForTests` completes a JSON-RPC roundtrip over a real `WebSocketServer` in `~14ms` — fix does not affect working connections.
  - **Production constant** is `30_000ms` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
  - **Vitest regression tests**: 6 passed, including negative control (CONNECTING hang) and initialize-timeout proof.

- **What was not tested:** Real Codex app-server with live Codex CLI; real Unix socket transport (tested via vitest mocks). The fix operates at the `ws` library `WebSocket.ClientOptions.handshakeTimeout` level — the standalone proof tests that boundary through the production `createWebSocketTransport` function with a real TCP server and real `ws` negotiation.
- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** the proof uses a short `testHooks.handshakeTimeoutMs: 200` to avoid wall-clock 30s waits; the production constant is verified via a separate assertion (`HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS === 30_000`). The hung peer intentionally accepts TCP and never completes the WS upgrade to simulate a broken/evil peer scenario.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The fix adds a `handshakeTimeout` option to WebSocket construction that was previously omitted. The `ws` library already supports this option (documented). The 30s default matches established gateway handshake floors. `perMessageDeflate: false` is preserved. The `listenerCount` guard on error re-emit prevents unhandled-error crashes when callers only subscribe to `exit`, which is the correct behavior for handshake hang paths.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where edge-case Control UI preview inputs and assistant media filenames were accepted more broadly than needed, which could produce unnecessary upstream requests or less predictable download headers.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change tightens shared object-key filtering, validates GitHub preview repository names before any preview fetch, normalizes GitHub avatar URLs to a small deterministic request shape, and sanitizes assistant media filenames before building response headers. The patch keeps the existing Control UI and config merge behavior for valid inputs.

## User Impact

Users should see the same behavior for normal GitHub issue and pull request previews and normal assistant media downloads. Invalid preview targets, unsafe avatar URLs, and unusual media filenames are now handled more conservatively.

target.title: fix(provider-runtime): treat HTTP 429 as retryable in provider operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) is not recognized as a retryable error in provider operations outside the chat completion path. When media providers (image generation, speech synthesis, video generation) return HTTP 429, the operation fails immediately instead of retrying with backoff.

Root cause: two separate transient HTTP status classifiers each omitted 429:

- `isTransientProviderOperationError` in `src/provider-runtime/operation-retry.ts:154` — the generic retry-loop classifier
- `isTransientProviderHttpStatus` in `src/media-understanding/shared.ts:644` — the guarded POST retry gate used by `postJsonRequest`, `postTranscriptionRequest`, and `postMultipartRequest`

Both checked only 500/502/503/504. A retry-enabled POST receiving 429 was returned past the retry scope without retrying. The chat completion path is unaffected because it uses `executeWithApiKeyRotation` with `isApiKeyRateLimitError` for key rotation on 429.

Relates to gap finding: `ctx-media-429-retry-missing` (`manual-discovery`, evidence level A)
Location: `src/provider-runtime/operation-retry.ts:154`

## Why This Change Was Made

Unify both transient status classifiers: add `status === 429 ||` to the `isTransientProviderHttpStatus` POST gate (shared.ts) so it matches the generic classifier (operation-retry.ts). Add `429|` to the message regex in `isTransientProviderOperationError`.

Add a caller-level regression test at the `postJsonRequest` → `postGuardedRequest` → `isTransientProviderHttpStatus` boundary that proves a retry-enabled POST 429 response throws into the retry loop and succeeds on retry.

This is the best fix: share one canonical transient status set between both decision points. 429 is inherently a transient error like 5xx server errors.

### Scope boundary

This PR is scoped to **classification only** — adding 429 to the transient error classifiers so the existing retry loop engages. `Retry-After` header parsing and provider-specific rate-limit window awareness is out of scope here; the existing 5xx retry paths have the same limitation and would be addressed as a separate enhancement.

## User Impact

Users of media providers (image generation, speech synthesis, video generation) and other read/analysis POST endpoints: previously, 429 rate limits caused immediate failure; after this fix, operations retry automatically with backoff per the provider retry configuration. This applies to both direct retry-loop callers and guarded POST operations (transcription, JSON POST reads, multipart reads). Billable create operations remain excluded from default retry. No effect on other provider operations.

## Evidence

- 4 files, +56/-3 lines (source +2/-2 net 0, shared.ts +1/-1 net 0, tests +53)
- Source diff: add `status === 429 ||` and `429|` to both transient classifiers; add 429 to `isTransientProviderHttpStatus`

### Unit tests (61 passed, 2 files)

```
$ pnpm test src/provider-runtime/operation-retry.test.ts src/media-understanding/shared.test.ts

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  61 passed (61)
```

**operation-retry.test.ts (16 passed)**: 2 new parameterized 429 cases — structured `{ status: 429 }` and unstructured `HTTP 429` message — both retried correctly. Network-failure retry cases, negative controls (400, ENOENT) still fail-fast, create-stage exclusion intact.

**shared.test.ts (45 passed)**: 1 new caller-level regression test — "retries read JSON POST 429 rate limit responses" — exercises `postJsonRequest` with `retryStage: "read"` where first response is 429 and second is 200. Proves:
- 429 POST response is classified as transient by `isTransientProviderHttpStatus` and throws into the retry loop
- `executeProviderOperationWithRetry` re-issues the operation
- Second response (200) succeeds
- First response body is released after the error is thrown
- `sleep` delay is honored

### Real behavior proof: live HTTP 429 retry loop

Local HTTP server returns 429 on first request and 200 on second, exercising `executeProviderOperationWithRetry` with a real `fetch` call. The retry loop correctly classifies the 429 response as transient, waits for backoff, and succeeds on the retry.

```
=== HTTP 429 Retry Proof ===

[setup] Local HTTP server listening on http://127.0.0.1:45081

--- Result ---
  ✓ Retry loop succeeded on attempt 2
  Response: {"status":"ok","attempt":2}

--- Timing ---
  Attempt 1: 2026-07-14T06:31:16.678Z
  Retry   2: 2026-07-14T06:31:16.861Z (+183ms)
  Total elapsed: 183ms
  Retry config: attempts=2, baseDelayMs=100, maxDelayMs=500

--- Verdict ---
  ✓ Real 429 → retry → 200 success: retry loop engaged correctly.
  ✓ Retry delay 183ms ≥ baseDelayMs 100ms: backoff honored.
```

This proves:
- Real HTTP 429 responses are classified as transient and trigger the retry loop
- The retry delay (183ms with baseDelayMs=100, or 500ms with default baseDelayMs=250) ensures the second request falls outside the immediate rate-limit window
- The second request succeeds with 200, completing the provider operation
- The existing exponential backoff mechanism controls retry timing (`maxDelayMs=1000` caps the 2nd-attempt delay at 1s)

target.title: feat: AI safety event taxonomy — core event contracts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
OpenClaw has operational diagnostics, OTEL exporters, and prompt-injection hardening, but no first-class AI safety/quality event taxonomy. Without a shared schema, safety signals (prompt injection attempts, tool policy decisions, external content ingestion, eval scores) are invisible to operators and cannot be correlated across sessions or exported consistently.

## Evidence
- `src/infra/diagnostic-events.ts` — `DiagnosticSecurityEvent.category` enum confirms no `ai_safety` category exists in main
- Clawsweeper review of issue #82548 (June 29) confirmed current main does not have the requested taxonomy
- New types: `ai_safety.prompt_injection.signal`, `ai_safety.tool_policy.decision`, `ai_safety.external_content.consumed`, `ai_safety.user_feedback.received`, `ai_safety.memory_context.selected`, `ai_safety.eval.result`
- 8 unit tests added in `src/infra/diagnostic-events.test.ts` covering each new event type and schema version constant
- Depends on: nothing (this is the unblocking schema PR)
- Unblocks: #107184 (exporters), #107187 (plugin API), #107192 (UI/CLI)

## Evidence — Clawsweeper re-review fixes (2026-07-14)

**Security fix:** `DiagnosticAISafetyEventPayload` is now excluded from `DiagnosticEventInput` (the untrusted `emitDiagnosticEvent()` surface). AI safety events are emittable only via the trusted core path (`emitTrustedDiagnosticEvent`, new `TrustedDiagnosticEventInput` type) or the policy-gated `emitPluginSafetyEvent` from #107187. A runtime gate mirroring the existing `security.event` gate additionally drops any `ai_safety.*` event emitted untrusted, so plugins cannot spoof safety findings even with an unsafe cast. Contract tests moved to `src/infra/diagnostic-ai-safety-events.test.ts` and now cover the untrusted-drop behavior:

```

✓ diagnostic AI safety events > all six AI safety event types carry standard seq/ts enrichment

Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

**4-PR series design note:** the security boundary is deliberate across the stack — this PR defines the contracts and locks the untrusted path; #107184 wires exporters and preserves emitter provenance; #107187 adds the only plugin-facing emission surface, gated by manifest `safetyEventTypes`; #107192 adds observability surfaces. Untrusted path gated, trusted path only.

**OTEL note:** full end-to-end OTEL integration proof requires a running collector, which is not available in CI; exporter behavior is covered by unit tests in #107184.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(codex): continue after source-reply delivery instead of terminating turn
target.body:
Fixes #106961

## Summary

Codex-backed agent turns prematurely terminated after an intermediate source-reply message send, preventing subsequent tool execution; this fix removes the implicit terminate-on-delivery classification so the turn continues until the normal Codex turn/completed lifecycle.
- Problem: In `message_tool_only` mode, a successful message-tool send to the source channel set `terminate=true` on the dynamic tool response, causing `scheduleTurnReleaseAfterTerminalDynamicTool` to interrupt the turn before subsequent tools could execute.
- Solution: Remove `deliveredSourceReply` and `receiptConfirmedSourceReply` from the `withDynamicToolTermination` conditions; only an explicit `final=true` argument now terminates the turn, matching the generic embedded-runner behavior from PR #92343.
- What changed: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.ts` (terminate classification + sourceReplyFinal telemetry), `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts` (updated assertions + new regression test)
- What did NOT change: `shouldReleaseTurnAfterTerminalDynamicTool`, `resolveTerminalDynamicToolBatchAction`, `shouldBlockTerminalReleaseForNonTerminalDynamicToolResult`, generic embedded-runner suppression logic, finalize path, any config/env/schema surface

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related #106961
- Related #92343 (prior generic fix establishing the desired behavior)
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Issue #106961 reports a Codex-specific recurrence of premature message-tool turn termination on v2026.7.1. The prior generic fix (PR #92343, commit `4620929`) corrected the embedded runner to continue after source-reply delivery, but PR #95942 (commit `9b9a124c`) re-introduced the same termination behavior in the Codex app-server path. Commit `4dc6e182c3` further hardened the incorrect "degrade to terminate-on-delivery when `final` is omitted" logic. This regression breaks Discord/Codex workflows where an agent sends an acknowledgment ("One moment") and then needs to execute further tools.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

**Behavior addressed**: Codex dynamic tool bridge terminates the turn immediately after a successful source-reply message send, preventing subsequent tool calls in the same turn.

**Real environment tested**: Linux, Node v24.13.1, branch `fix/codex-source-reply-terminate-106961`

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

```bash
node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/vitest run \
  extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
```

Runs the actual OpenClaw vitest suite against the patched `createCodexDynamicToolBridge` runtime, not a copied classifier. This is the same test file and runtime the CI uses.

**Evidence after fix**:

```console
$ node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/vitest run \
  extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose | tail -30

 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not mark delivered
   message-tool-only source replies as terminal when final is omitted
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > requires explicit
   final=true to make a delivered message-tool-only source reply terminal
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > continues after an
   intermediate message-tool-only source reply without final
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not deliver
   message-tool-only source replies as delivered telemetry …
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not mark explicit
   message-tool sends as terminal source replies
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > does not mark mismatched
   explicit message-tool sends as terminal source replies
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > records message-tool-owned
   terminal replies as delivered source replies

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  100 passed (100)
```

All 100 tests pass. Key regression test "continues after an intermediate message-tool-only source reply without final" validates the exact #106961 scenario: intermediate message → subsequent exec call → both with terminate=undefined.

**Observed result after fix**:

1. Intermediate message-tool-only source replies (final omitted) no longer set terminate=true
2. sourceReplyFinal telemetry remains true when final is omitted for delivered/receipt source replies — preserves completed marker for stranded-reply recovery (no duplicate replay on error/timeout)
3. Receipt-confirmed source replies (final omitted) no longer set terminate=true
4. Explicit final=true + actual source reply delivery still terminates the turn
5. Cross-channel message-tool sends with final=true do NOT terminate (not a source reply)
6. Tool-returned terminate:true (toolConfirmedSourceReply) still terminates unless overridden by final=false
7. Yield results still terminate correctly
8. didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool and messagingToolSourceReplyPayloads are still correctly collected

**What was not tested**: Live Discord/Codex run with a real Codex-backed agent; requires Crabbox/Testbox + Discord credential. stranding-recovery duplicate protection relies on sourceReplyFinal=true remained consistent — the Completed marker is preserved so recovery will not re-deliver an already-successful message.

## Root Cause

PR #95942 (commit `9b9a124c`) added Codex app-server source-reply support by including `deliveredSourceReply` and `receiptConfirmedSourceReply` in the `withDynamicToolTermination` conditions. This re-introduced the premature termination that PR #92343 (commit `4620929`) had just removed from the generic embedded runner. Commit `4dc6e182c3` further hardened the incorrect "final omitted → degrade to terminate-on-delivery" fallback, making the regression harder to detect.

## Regression Test Plan

- `pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts` — covers all source-reply terminate scenarios including the new "continues after an intermediate message-tool-only source reply without final" test
- `pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts` — covers shouldReleaseTurnAfterTerminalDynamicTool (unchanged by this fix)
- `pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.dynamic-tools.test.ts` — covers terminal diagnostics (unchanged)
- `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/message-tool-terminal.test.ts` — covers generic hook behavior (unchanged)
- `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe*.test.ts` — covers duplicate-output suppression (unchanged)

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Codex-backed Discord agents will no longer stop executing after sending an intermediate acknowledgment message. The agent will continue the turn, executing subsequent tools and delivering the final result, matching the behavior of the generic embedded runner.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes — correcting the Codex terminal classification to match the established generic source-reply contract is the narrowest fix that addresses the regression without introducing new surfaces.
- **Refactor needed**: No
- **Alternative considered**: Adding a new config option to control terminate-on-delivery was rejected per AGENTS.md "Config/env surface bar is high" and the Codex review's explicit requirement "without adding a new config option or parallel message schema."

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **AI model**: glm-5.1
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes
- **AI prompts / session excerpts**: Issue analysis, source code tracing across dynamic-tools.ts, embedded-agent-subscribe.ts, agent-loop.ts, and upstream Codex protocol (codex-rs/protocol/src/dynamic_tools.rs)

## Risks and Mitigations

**Highest-risk area**: Duplicate channel messages after fix — if the generic-layer suppression (`suppressMessageToolOnlySourceReplyOutput`) does not correctly receive the `didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool` flag, the agent could send both the intermediate message and the final output to the source channel.

**Mitigation**: The `didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool` and `messagingToolSourceReplyPayloads` collection occurs before `withDynamicToolTermination` in the code path and is not gated by the `terminate` flag. The generic suppression layer checks `messagingToolSourceReplyPayloads.length > 0` to activate suppression, which remains correct. However, this needs verification via `pnpm test src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe*.test.ts` in a full build environment.

**Compatibility impact**: Backward compatible. No config/env changes. No new schema. The only behavior change is that intermediate source-reply messages no longer terminate the turn, which is the intended behavior per PR #92343.

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes
- [x] Config/env changes? No
- [x] Migration needed? No

target.title: fix(policy): reject nondecimal watch interval
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `policy watch --interval-ms` accepted JavaScript-specific coercion forms — leading plus (`+500`), leading zeros (`0500`), or longer zero-padded spellings (`000500`) — silently normalizing them to a different but valid integer before reaching the polling loop. Operators resuming from a documented decimal `intervalMs` could therefore request an unintended cadence through a non-canonical alias the parser still accepted.

## Why This Change Was Made

The watch-interval parser now uses the shared `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` and additionally enforces a decimal-only envelope (trimmed input must equal `String(raw)`) so JS coercion forms are rejected at the CLI boundary. Canonical decimal values, the default of `2000`, and the documented lower bound of `250` continue to route unchanged.

This mirrors the canonical sibling `extensions/google-meet/src/cli.ts` (which uses `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` for `--since`) and the broader Wave 1 strict-parser cohort (#106384, #106926, #105557), and adds the decimal-only envelope because `--interval-ms` is documented as a decimal rather than an opaque cursor.

## User Impact

`policy watch --interval-ms` now only accepts canonical decimal non-negative integers. Plus-prefixed, leading-zero-padded, and non-decimal spellings fail fast with the existing `--interval-ms must be an integer >= 250.` message instead of reaching the polling loop as a different cadence. The default `2000`, the boundary `250`, and every previously accepted documented decimal interval are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Before fix (FAIL on pinned main `7b16b35cb3`)

```text
 FAIL  |extensions| extensions/policy/src/cli.test.ts > policy commands > rejects noncanonical plus-prefixed and leading-zero policy watch intervals before evaluating policy
AssertionError: interval=+500: expected 1 to be 2 // Object.is equality

- Expected: 2
+ Received: 1

  at extensions/policy/src/cli.test.ts:384:45

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 33 passed (34)
```

### After fix (PASS on patched head)

```text

   Duration  9.86s
```

### Focused regression

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/policy/src/cli.test.ts` — 34/34 passed (33 existing + 1 new `rejects noncanonical plus-prefixed and leading-zero policy watch intervals` covering `+500`, `+250`, `0500`, `000500`).
- `git diff --check` — clean.

### Local CLI smoke deferral

Local Node 22.22.0 is below the required 22.22.3 floor, so the `pnpm openclaw policy watch …` launcher refuses to spawn. The vitest `runPolicyWatchJson({ intervalMs: "+500" })` path exercises the canonical `registerPolicyCli(program)` + `program.parseAsync(["policy", "watch", "--interval-ms", "+500", "--once", "--json"])` end-to-end — same code path the launcher invokes on a supported Node. Hosted Testbox will run the full CLI smoke.

### What was NOT changed

- `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` shared helper — left as-is so opaque numeric cursors in other extensions (google-meet `--since`, etc.) keep their permissive `+`/leading-zero coercion.
- Default `2000` and lower bound `250` for `--interval-ms`.
- Existing error message string.
- Config, schema, protocol, plugin SDK, plugin manifest, or runtime hooks.
- Any other `--interval-ms` consumer outside `extensions/policy/src/cli.ts`.

## Risk / Compatibility

🚨 compatibility: `+500`, `0500`, and `000500` were silently accepted as `500` by the old parser; they are now rejected at the CLI boundary. No documented decimal interval (`2000`, `250`, `500`, etc.) is affected. Canonical decimal values continue to route unchanged.

- #106926 — `fix(onepassword): validate audit limit strictly`
- #105557 — `fix(cli): reject noncanonical trajectory export requests`

target.title: fix(plugins): restore nested registry state on failed registration rollback
target.body:
Fixes #106647

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a failed plugin registration could leave nested registry state partially applied. OpenClaw snapshots the plugin registry for transactional rollback, but the snapshot only copied top-level arrays and maps while keeping references to nested `PluginRecord` objects and existing capability entries. During registration, the loader mutates those objects in place (for example appending `toolNames` or extending middleware `runtimes`). On rollback, the array structure was restored while the mutated nested fields remained, so a failed plugin load could poison later retries and leave inconsistent registry metadata.

## Why This Change Was Made

Registration rollback now isolates transaction-owned mutable state without cloning the entire registry with `structuredClone` (which would break function-bearing handlers). Array and record entries get property-level snapshots that clone mutable arrays/values while keeping handlers by reference. The live `PluginRecord` being registered is included even before it is pushed onto `registry.plugins`, and all loader registration transactions pass that record through. This keeps one canonical rollback path, preserves executable handlers, and restores counters/lists after failure.

Fix quality: compatibility — no config/API change, runtime-only isolation; performance — snapshot cost only at registration boundaries, not request hot paths; usability — failed loads no longer leave sticky partial metadata; security — no trust-boundary change, fail closed still rolls back side effects.

## User Impact

Operators and developers who hit a plugin registration failure during load, setup-runtime registration, or CLI metadata registration get a clean rollback of plugin records and nested capability entries. A retry after a failed registration starts from the pre-failure registry state instead of carrying over tool names, route counters, errors, or middleware runtime lists from the failed attempt.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

Focused tests (primary surface):

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts
 ✓ |plugins| src/plugins/plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts (4 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

Regression coverage added for:

1. Restoring the live current `PluginRecord` after failed registration (`toolNames`, `httpRoutes`, `hookCount`, `contextEngineIds`, `error`).
2. Restoring in-place mutations on existing middleware registrations (`runtimes`) while preserving handler function identity and required `source` metadata.

Closeout notes: `pnpm changed:lanes` / path-scoped oxlint stalled or expanded on this host; substituted with `git diff --check`, `pnpm exec oxfmt` on the three touched files, and the focused Vitest path above (quality floor met).

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Failed plugin registration rollback no longer retains nested in-place mutations on `PluginRecord` counters/lists or existing capability entries such as agent tool-result middleware `runtimes`.
- Environment: local macOS 15, OpenClaw checkout at this PR head, Node via repo Vitest plugins config.
- Current-main contrast: On main, `snapshotPluginRegistry` does `[...array]` / `{...object}` only. Mutating `record.toolNames.push(...)` or `middleware.runtimes.push(...)` during a transaction leaves those mutations after `rollback()` because nested object identity is shared. This PR clones mutable property values and restores the live current record plus registry entry clones.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts -t "restores the current record|restores in-place"
  ```
- Evidence after fix: both targeted cases pass; after rollback, `record.toolNames` is `[]` with a new array identity, counters reset, optional `error` removed; middleware entry is a new object with original `rawHandler`/`handler` identity and `runtimes: ["openclaw"]` (not including a pushed `"codex"`).
- Control check: pre-existing rollback of top-level registry writes and non-activating commit behavior still pass in the same file (4/4). Handler identity equality proves functions were not structured-cloned away.
- Observed result after fix: registration transaction rollback fully restores nested mutable state for the current record and for pre-existing registry entries.
- What was not tested: live multi-plugin install with a deliberately broken third-party package in a production gateway process; that path uses the same `createPluginRegistrationTransaction` call sites updated in `loader.ts` and is covered at the transaction boundary here.

## AI disclosure

This PR was authored with AI assistance (Grok).

target.title: fix(deepinfra): use OpenAI video end point and tag DeepSeek thinking format
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Two user-visible DeepInfra integration problems: **Video generation.** Fixes an issue where generating video through the DeepInfra provider used DeepInfra's legacy native inference path and a small, hardcoded set of video models. Newly released DeepInfra video models (Veo 3.1, Wan 2.x, Pixverse, Seedance, …) never appeared, and the video surface didn't behave like OpenClaw's other DeepInfra modalities (chat, image, speech), which already run over DeepInfra's OpenAI-compatible API. DeepInfra has since shipped an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/openai/videos` endpoint and tagged its video models, so the catalog can be discovered live. **DeepSeek replies.** Fixes an issue where chatting with a DeepInfra DeepSeek model (e.g. DeepSeek-V4-Flash) leaked the model's raw reasoning/tool-call markup — `<|DSML|…>` and `reasoning_content` — into the visible reply, and could drop tool calls. Because DeepInfra serves every model family over a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, OpenClaw treated DeepSeek as a generic "openai" model and never recovered its DeepSeek-dialect output. ## Why This Change Was Made - **Video** now targets DeepInfra's async `/v1/openai/videos` job endpoint (submit → poll → result URL), matching the other OpenAI-compatible surfaces, and builds its model list from live discovery filtered by the `video-gen` tag, with a small static fallback when no API key is configured. Scope: text-to-video only (image/video reference inputs remain unsupported). - **DeepSeek** is declared with `thinkingFormat: "deepseek"` for the `deepseek-ai/*` family (the same per-family dialect approach already used for Qwen), so core strips/recovers DeepSeek's `reasoning_content` and DSML tool calls instead of passing them through; models carrying the `reasoning` / `reasoning_effort` tag are marked reasoning-capable so thinking levels apply. ## User Impact - **Video:** Users get the current DeepInfra text-to-video catalog, auto-discovered (no more stale hardcoded list), generated through the same OpenAI-compatible flow as the other modalities. No config or workflow change needed. - **DeepSeek:** DeepSeek models on DeepInfra now return clean replies — no leaked `<|DSML|…>` / reasoning markup — tool calls work reliably, and reasoning / "thinking" levels are honored. ## Evidence Verified live on a hosted OpenClaw instance running this branch (DeepInfra provider; agent model `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash`), driven via `openclaw agent`, with outbound HTTP captured at the network layer. **1 — Video uses the new endpoint + tag discovery.** Captured request timeline across two generations: - `GET /v1/openai/models?sort_by=openclaw&filter=with_meta` → 200 — tag discovery (returns 13 `video-gen` models: Veo 3.1/-fast, Wan 2.6/2.2-T2V, Pixverse-6 / T2V / T2V-HD, Seedance 2.0 / 1.5-Pro, Cosmos3, LTX2, p-video) - `POST /v1/openai/videos` → 200 — async submit (returns a `videos_` job) - `GET /v1/openai/videos/videos_` → 200, polled ~every 5 s until succeeded - **zero `/v1/inference` calls**; - MP4s rendered and attached to the reply. _📸 Screenshot: `capture_events` timeline (POST /v1/openai/videos + polls)_ https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1bc82632-378f-4f90-bf4d-f84ac915ff40 **2 — DeepSeek thinking format.** - `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash` discovery tags: `["chat","prompt_cache","reasoning"]` - `openclaw agent --thinking high` on a reasoning prompt → correct step-by-step answer with **no `<|DSML|…>` / `reasoning_content` in the reply**, even though the DeepInfra response body did contain a `reasoning_content` field (confirmed in the capture) — i.e. it's recovered, not leaked. _📸 Screenshot: clean DeepSeek reasoning reply_ [request.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29214104/request.json) Focused provider tests cover the video submit→poll→result flow (success, immediate-success, job failure, malformed payloads) and the DeepSeek-family tagging.

target.title: fix: resolve Tavily SecretRefs in agent tools
target.body:
Fixes #95109

## Summary

- Select the active resolved runtime config snapshot in one shared helper before agent/plugin tool surfaces read credentials.
- Apply Tool Search defaults on top of that selected runtime config, so run-local overlays do not turn a resolved snapshot back into authored SecretRefs.
- Reuse the same selector from direct plugin-tool resolution and Tool Search resolution, avoiding drift between agent-visible plugin tools and direct plugin tools.
- Update Tavily's plugin-local API-key resolver to use inspect-mode SecretRef handling so a matching unresolved `env:*:TAVILY_API_KEY` ref can use the documented `process.env.TAVILY_API_KEY` fallback.
- Keep explicit non-env and nonmatching Tavily SecretRefs fail-closed instead of silently replacing file, exec, or other env refs with the ambient Tavily key.
- Add focused regressions for the agent Tool Search runtime snapshot path and the Tavily env fallback credential boundary.

## Root Cause

There were two related Tavily SecretRef failures at different ownership layers.

1. The agent Tool Search runtime-config overlay selected the wrong base config. The embedded attempt path and harness bridge applied local Tool Search defaults directly to `params.config`. When `params.config` was the authored source config, the overlay clone no longer matched the active runtime source snapshot, so later plugin-tool config selection treated it as explicit config and did not swap in the already-resolved runtime snapshot. Tavily then received an exec-backed SecretRef instead of the resolved in-memory string.
2. Tavily's plugin-local resolver used strict SecretRef normalization before the documented env fallback. `extensions/tavily/src/config.ts` called strict normalization on `plugins.entries.tavily.config.webSearch.apiKey`; an unresolved env SecretRef threw before `process.env.TAVILY_API_KEY` could be read.

RCA proof:

- Agent Tool Search before behavior: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts` and `src/agents/harness/tool-surface-bridge.ts` applied Tool Search defaults before runtime snapshot selection.
- Existing selector proof: direct plugin tools already used the source/runtime snapshot matching rule; this PR moves that rule into `src/agents/tool-runtime-config.ts` and reuses it.
- Tavily before behavior: `extensions/tavily/src/config.ts` used strict SecretRef normalization ahead of the env fallback, which matches the `UnresolvedSecretInputError` in #95109.
- Dependency contract inspected: `resolveSecretInputString` strict mode throws on unresolved refs; inspect mode returns ref metadata so the plugin can allow only the matching env fallback and block file/exec/wrong-env refs.

## What Problem This Solves

Users with Tavily configured through resolved runtime SecretRefs can use agent-visible Tavily tools without the Tool Search overlay reintroducing unresolved source SecretRefs.

Users with Tavily configured as `{ source: "env", provider: "default", id: "TAVILY_API_KEY" }` can also rely on the documented gateway environment fallback when that env ref is not inline-resolved in the current read-only plugin path. Tavily still does not silently borrow `TAVILY_API_KEY` for file refs, exec refs, or env refs targeting another variable.

## Why This Change Was Made

The agent runtime now chooses the applicable resolved runtime snapshot before applying local Tool Search defaults. That keeps run-local config overlays in memory, preserves the authored SecretRef in source config, and avoids storing plaintext credentials.

The Tavily plugin now mirrors the inspect-mode SecretRef pattern used by sibling web providers: it classifies configured secrets as available, missing, or blocked before deciding whether the ambient env fallback is allowed.

## User Impact

Agent-visible Tavily tools can use exec/file/env SecretRefs that have already been resolved into the active runtime snapshot.

Tavily also no longer throws before checking `TAVILY_API_KEY` for the canonical env SecretRef configuration reported in #95109. Explicit non-env Tavily SecretRefs remain fail-closed if unavailable.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior fixed: Tool Search runtime config now carries resolved in-memory Tavily API key values to agent/plugin tools while the source config keeps the authored SecretRef; Tavily's plugin-local resolver now allows the matching env SecretRef fallback without weakening file/exec/wrong-env credential boundaries.

Closest feasible environment tested: focused Vitest coverage through the actual agent Tool Search runtime helpers and Tavily resolver code, plus current-head terminal proof through the real `tavily_search` tool entrypoint. The current-head proof configured Tavily with an env SecretRef, set only a generated dummy `TAVILY_API_KEY`, and called the real Tavily endpoint. Tavily returned the expected dummy-key auth failure instead of OpenClaw throwing `UnresolvedSecretInputError`.

Current-head Tavily env SecretRef proof:

```text

# script imported createTavilySearchTool and resolveTavilyApiKey from this checkout
# cfg.plugins.entries.tavily.config.webSearch.apiKey = { source: "env", provider: "default", id: "TAVILY_API_KEY" }
# process.env.TAVILY_API_KEY = generated dummy value only
SCRIPT
```

Focused regression output:

- Current-head real behavior proof: redacted dummy-key `tavily_search` call against `https://api.tavily.com/search` reached Tavily and returned 401 instead of `UnresolvedSecretInputError`.

target.title: feat(config): add ordered config layers
target.body:
## What problem this solves

Hosts such as Lobster need to combine deployment-wide defaults, tenant-specific connectivity, and operator-local choices before starting OpenClaw. Today that composition happens outside OpenClaw by baking or mutating one `openclaw.json`, so OpenClaw cannot validate the original documents or enforce the authority boundary that produced the effective config.

This adds an official, opt-in way to start a Gateway from ordered ordinary OpenClaw config documents.

## Why core support instead of `$include` or launcher-side merging

`$include` is useful for assembling one authored config document. It does not express that an earlier source owns a value, reject a later source that tries to replace it, prove that later tool policy only tightens the effective policy, or make the resulting runtime immutable.

A launcher can implement those rules itself, but then it must duplicate OpenClaw's JSON5/include/env/schema/plugin validation and OpenClaw sees only the flattened result. That is the baked-overlay problem this PR is intended to remove.

The core addition is deliberately narrow: one repeatable CLI option, one recursive composer, and one startup-only/read-only lifecycle. It adds no config keys and no host-, tenant-, or operator-specific roles.

## User impact

No behavior changes unless `--config-layer` is supplied. Regular config users do not encounter this feature.

Opted-in Gateways use the composed snapshot for their lifetime. Config-mutating RPCs and persistence paths targeting that Gateway's canonical config are rejected, and config hot reload is disabled. Writes for unrelated config paths remain allowed. Restart with new source documents to activate a change.

## Example

Lobster can materialize three normal OpenClaw config files:

```json5
// scout-global.json5
{
  gateway: { mode: "local" },
  tools: { deny: ["exec"] },
}
```

```json5
// tenant-network.json5
{
  gateway: {
    controlUi: {
      allowedOrigins: ["https://scout.example.tenant"],
    },
  },
  tools: { deny: ["exec", "web"] },
}
```

```json5
// operator-local.json5
{
  logging: { level: "debug" },
}
```

Then start OpenClaw explicitly:

```bash
openclaw gateway run \
  --config-layer global=./scout-global.json5 \
  --config-layer tenant=./tenant-network.json5 \
  --config-layer operator=./operator-local.json5
```

The labels could be `one`, `two`, and `three`; only declaration order matters.

## Delivered V1

- repeat `--config-layer <id=path>` in precedence order
- parse through OpenClaw JSON5, include, env, schema, and plugin validation
- compose sparse documents recursively
- keep earlier exact values authoritative
- allow later `tools.allow` / `tools.deny` values only when they provably tighten policy
- keep the composed runtime startup-only and read-only
- scope persistence blocking to the layered Gateway's canonical config path
- treat pathless mutation preflights as targeting that canonical path, preventing plugin side effects before persistence

Layer IDs are descriptive only. Core has no built-in host, tenant, or operator roles.

## Evidence

Current PR head: `a7acafa0869`. Runtime-reviewed code head: `8dc592014ba01185adfa863b809702c62c3339c3`, rebased onto `578163c4a337fa7788252b1911d21680c2f6ccc9`. The head-only delta is documentation clarifying why OpenClaw owns composition semantics and how path-scoped writes behave.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/config-layers.test.ts src/config/nix-mode-write-guard.test.ts src/cli/gateway-cli/config-layers.test.ts src/gateway/server-methods/agents-mutate.test.ts`
- 63 focused tests pass
- mixed-owner regression proves a layered path does not block an unrelated config path
- pathless-preflight regression proves early plugin/doctor/update guards resolve to the canonical owned path
- `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passes
- final `codex review --base upstream/main`: no discrete actionable regression
- broader OpenClaw/Lobster prototype established the lifecycle constraints; this PR is the reduced startup-only slice
- Lobster fork adapter materializes the three files and launches OpenClaw with the repeated generic flags

Local `pnpm build` and direct `oxlint` invocations hung in this WSL worktree and were terminated; upstream CI is the authoritative broad build/lint result.

## Real behavior proof

The original foreground lifecycle proof established:

- Gateway logged `ready`; `GET /healthz` returned `{"ok":true,"status":"live"}`
- `config.get` returned the tenant origin, `tools.deny: ["exec", "web"]`, and operator `logging.level: "info"`
- `config.patch` rejected with `configuration writes are unavailable while --config-layer is active`
- a fourth layer replacing tenant `allowedOrigins` rejected with `ControlledByEarlierLayer`
- the canonical config path remained absent

After the ownership fix and rebase, two additional real Gateway lanes ran on the exact current head:

- fresh state: startup and health passed, layered values were effective, canonical `openclaw.json` remained absent
- existing state: startup and health passed, layered values were effective, and the pre-existing canonical file's SHA-256 and legacy `meta.lastTouchedVersion` marker remained byte-for-byte unchanged

Bundled and persisted plugin registries and channel/provider sidecars were disabled only to bound source-startup cost. Layer parsing, composition, Gateway activation, RPC reads, and persistence guards remained active.

## Scope and non-goals

Included:

- ordered recursive composition
- normal OpenClaw parsing and validation
- bounded tool-policy tightening
- immutable startup snapshot
- docs and a Lobster-shaped example

Not included:

- live layer reload
- write-through routing
- provenance/query APIs
- rollback generations
- special layer roles

## Ownership decision

OpenClaw should own ordered-layer composition semantics because it owns the schema, plugin-aware validation, tool-policy interpretation, runtime snapshot, and mutation boundary. Hosts should own only value materialization and source order. External flattening would erase authority before OpenClaw can enforce it and require each host to duplicate OpenClaw-specific behavior.

This remains a draft pending maintainer sponsorship of that bounded core contract.

Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/34

target.body:
## Summary

AI-assisted PR.

- Problem: OpenAI-compatible embedding providers passed raw query text to instruction-aware embedding models such as Qwen3, Nomic, and mxbai.
- Why it matters: Raw queries produced lower-quality retrieval for instruction-aware embedding models because query embeddings did not match the model's expected retrieval-query format.
- What changed: OpenAI embeddings now apply model-specific query instruction prefixes for query embeddings, while document batch embeddings remain unchanged.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): No embedding defaults, credentials handling, base URL behavior, document embedding inputs, or non-OpenAI providers were changed.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature

- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [x] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #
- Related #
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** OpenAI-compatible embedding providers now apply model-specific query instruction prefixes for instruction-aware Qwen3, Nomic, and Mixedbread embedding model families on query embeddings, while document/batch embeddings remain raw.

**Real environment tested:** Local OpenClaw development checkout at PR head `65a5ce21910de9a43be7bed4ff1d22ab3f757b4b`, using configured model `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B` against an OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint on coedo. A local redacting/proof proxy only rewrote the model id for backend compatibility and captured the request bodies emitted by the providers.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Ran `tmp/pr-79702-current-head-proof.mts` from the PR worktree after the current-head rebase. The script exercised both touched provider paths: bundled OpenAI query/document embeddings and generic `openai-compatible` query/document embeddings.

**Evidence after fix:** Copied live terminal/request-capture output from the current-head proof run:

**What was not tested:** Every OpenAI-compatible embedding server and additional instruction-aware model families beyond the covered Qwen3, Nomic, and Mixedbread matchers were not tested.

- Integration/channel (if any): OpenClaw memorySearch

### Steps

2. Run the same 24-query live retrieval evaluation before and after the adapter change.
3. Compare top-3 recall and observed query latency in that setup.

### Actual

## Evidence

## Human Verification (required)

- Verified scenarios: Live memorySearch evaluation before and after the query-prefix change; unit tests for prefixed query embeddings and raw document embeddings.
- Edge cases checked: Empty input still returns an empty result; unknown models continue using raw queries; blank configured models still fall back to the default embedding model.
- What you did **not** verify: Every OpenAI-compatible embedding server or additional instruction-aware model family beyond the covered prefixes.
